function.name: probe_b200

reasoning_details.text:
I'm planning the budget carefully—6 GPU calls for compile and test, 12 turns total, with probes not counting against GPU calls. For the fat tiling approach, I'm thinking about having each half-warp handle multiple rows instead of one, which would reduce the CTA count significantly compared to the parent implementation's 49152 CTAs.

I'm working out the register budget and occupancy tradeoffs: with R=4 rows per half-warp, roughly 56 registers per thread lets me fit 4 CTAs per SM for 1024 threads and 128KB of data in flight, while R=2 would use fewer registers but less parallelism per thread. I also need to account for token counts that aren't evenly divisible by R, requiring masking for odd batch-sequence sizes like 131 or 586.

I'm planning a probe kernel parameterized by R to test different tokens-per-half-warp values against the baseline R=1 case across several data sizes, comparing thread counts and CTA grid sizes to see which configuration performs best.

I should check the probe's help output first to avoid guessing wrong about tensor/pointer types, then build the kernel source with a macro for R so I can compile separate variants via NVRTC targeting sm_100.

Writing kernel signature...

I'm working out how to map thread indices to head groups and token blocks: with THREADS/16 half-warps per block handling distinct heads, I need to generalize head-per-block and group counts so each half-warp computes the right row offset into the 48-head layout.

For tail handling with partial token counts (like 131 tokens with R=4), I just mask the invalid rows in the last block, and I'm planning to add store eviction hints before writing a quick probe to test timing across different token sizes starting at 128.

I'm sketching a sweep plan: test token counts from 128 up to 8192 against several R/THREADS configurations, totaling about 42 timing runs that should comfortably fit within the time budget even with large memory allocations at the biggest size. Given the limited number of turns available, I want to first check the probe API documentation before running the actual timing sweep.

function.name: probe_b200

reasoning_details.text:
I'm wondering if the fat tile slowdown is a DRAM page locality issue from jumping addresses, and considering an alternative layout where each CTA processes consecutive 16-row tiles contiguously instead.

Occupancy math suggests fat tiles should have more bytes in flight per SM than the parent, yet it's still slower—possibly due to tail imbalance from fewer concurrent CTAs finishing serially. I want to test a few layout variants next: contiguous tile grouping per CTA, a looped version with prefetching, and an interleaved grid-stride scheme that keeps the resident working set contiguous across CTAs like the one-shot approach naturally does.

I should also check register-capped occupancy via launch_bounds, and recall that the archive already tried token-block tiling on A100 with worse results than the current best—so that path is likely a dead end. The underlying issue seems tied to how the massive grid of CTAs spans memory.

I'm generalizing to a contiguous-row kernel where each CTA handles a block of rows and threads stride across them, computing head index as row mod 48 and masking out-of-range rows, plus a strided variant where threads load rows across a grid stride. I plan to test configs like (256,1), (512,1), (1024,1), and (256,2) for tile size and rows-per-thread.

Now I'm also considering launch bounds and register spill tradeoffs for configs like (128,2), (256,3), and strided variants (256,2), (256,4), plus treating Q and K as a combined virtual row space where row index determines which pointer to use, with per-row selection handling cases where 64-row tiles cross the Q/K boundary since n_rows isn't a multiple of 64.

function.name: probe_b200

reasoning_details.text:
The fatter config doesn't seem to be winning since CTA overhead isn't on the critical path here, and minBlocks enforcement isn't the issue either—48 registers at MINB 4 looks fine. The timing differences I'm seeing between configs (114.5 vs 115.9, 115.6) are small enough to be noise. I'm starting to suspect the real bottleneck is DRAM-related, possibly from write behavior, so I should look for a different angle to actually beat the baseline.

I'm considering a fat variant with 256 threads at R=2 contiguous and 48 registers, giving 5 CTAs per SM. Since reducing CTAs isn't helping, maybe the limiting factor is something like DRAM read/write turnaround—at 805MB the kernel nearly matches a plain copy, suggesting we're already at the ceiling there. The promising configs seem to be around 8192 with 512 threads, so I want to re-measure those more carefully with repeated, interleaved runs to rule out noise, and also try a few more register/thread combos (512/2, 384 threads) plus revisit the QK-pairing idea, though that already showed no gain. Let me run a noise-check probe before drawing conclusions.

function.name: run_tests

reasoning_details.text:
Testing 512 threads with 32 rows per CTA shows roughly 1-1.3% speedup on large token counts but a 4.5% slowdown on medium sizes, while 256 threads performs better on medium and small sizes. This suggests a dispatch rule: use 512 threads only when tokens exceed about 3000, otherwise stick with the default config — though the gain is marginal, and oddly 768 threads performs terribly for reasons I'm not sure of yet.

With 32 registers, 768 threads only fits 2 CTAs per SM (1536 threads total), lowering occupancy, whereas 512 threads allows 4 CTAs for full 2048-thread occupancy — that explains the gap. The 1024-token slowdown with 512 threads seems tied to wave quantization: both 256 and 512 thread configs produce roughly the same number of waves (5.19), but the larger granularity of 512 threads causes worse scheduling at certain sizes. Testing 2048 tokens confirms 512 is worse there too, so I'm settling on a threshold of 4096+ tokens to use 512 threads, since my target workloads (4096, 6184, 6628, 8192) all fall into that large band anyway. I also need to check that row indexing for Q/K tiles stays divisible correctly across token counts — all target sizes are even multiples that satisfy the 32-row tile boundary requirement.

Since 2*n_rows is always divisible by 32, I realize masking isn't needed in the kernel — just a cheap per-thread selection to determine whether a row belongs to Q or K. I'm keeping the parent's existing S-band loading policy for token counts at or below the threshold, and introducing the new 512-thread config only for the large band, implemented as a templated kernel parameterized by thread count and load policy. Now I just need to write this out, compile it, and run the test suite.
